subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Assalamu alaikum, and welcome to one of the most exciting units in your science year. In this unit you will study the physics of the world you live in every single day, from the tiniest trembling of the air to the enormous movements of the whole planet. We call this Earth physics because it connects three big ideas: how sound is made and travels, what the Earth is made of on the inside, and how the Sun, Moon and Earth move together to create eclipses. These may sound like three separate topics, but they are all about the same thing: how energy and matter behave in the world around you.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Describe the vibration of particles in a sound wave and explain why sound does not travel in a vacuum.
Explain echoes in terms of the reflection of sound waves.
Describe the model of plate tectonics, in which a solid outer layer (made up of the crust and uppermost mantle) moves because of flow lower in the mantle.
Describe how earthquakes, volcanoes and fold mountains occur near the boundaries of tectonic plates.
Explain how solar and lunar eclipses happen.

outcomes: Explain that sound is made by vibrations and describe how those vibrations start.
Describe how a sound wave travels by making particles vibrate backwards and forwards.
State that sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases, but not through a vacuum, and explain why.
Describe how sound waves are reflected to make echoes, and give useful and unwanted examples.
Distinguish between loudness (volume) and pitch, and connect each to the vibration.
Describe the structure of the Earth: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
Explain the evidence for continental drift and describe tectonic plates.
Explain how fold mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes form at plate boundaries.
Explain how the Sun, Moon and Earth produce solar and lunar eclipses.
State clearly why you must never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse.

concepts.title: How Sound Is Made
concepts.explanation:
Let us begin with something you have heard every day of your life: sound. Close your eyes for a moment and imagine the sounds around you right now. Perhaps you can hear voices, a goat bleating outside, the wind moving through an acacia tree, or a cooking pot being placed on the fire. Every one of these sounds started in exactly the same way: something vibrated.

To vibrate means to move backwards and forwards very quickly. When something vibrates, it pushes against the air around it and makes a sound. Think of the men playing the drum at a celebration. When a drummer strikes the skin of the drum, the tight surface moves up and down very fast, too fast for your eyes to follow. That fast movement is the vibration, and the vibration is what makes the sound you hear. If the drummer hits the drum with more force, the skin vibrates further and the sound becomes louder. If they tap it gently, the skin barely moves and the sound is soft.

You can feel a vibration in your own body. Place two fingers gently on the front of your throat and say your name out loud, or softly recite 'Bismillah'. Can you feel the gentle buzzing? That buzzing comes from your vocal cords, two small flaps inside your throat that vibrate when you speak. When you stop speaking, the vibration stops and so does the sound. This simple test proves an important rule: no vibration means no sound.

The same idea explains many musical instruments. A guitar or an oud makes a sound because its strings vibrate when you pluck them. It is not the wood, or the metal parts, or the air trapped inside that makes the note, it is the vibrating string. A loudspeaker in a radio or phone has a paper cone inside that vibrates in and out. If you place tiny grains of rice on a loudspeaker while music plays, the grains jump and bounce, showing you the cone is vibrating even when the movement is too small to see clearly.

Loudness and Pitch — Two Different Things

Not all sounds are the same, and scientists describe sound using two separate ideas that you must not mix up: loudness and pitch. Loudness (also called volume) is how loud or quiet a sound is. It depends on how much the object vibrates, or how big the vibration is. A big vibration carries more energy, so it makes a louder sound. This is why hitting a drum harder, or plucking a string with more force, makes the sound louder.

Pitch is different. Pitch is how high or low a sound is. Thunder rolling over the Rift Valley is a low-pitched sound. A baby crying, a whistle, or a small bird is a high-pitched sound. Pitch depends on how fast something vibrates: fast vibrations make high sounds, and slow vibrations make low sounds. A thin, tight guitar string vibrates quickly and gives a high note, while a thick, loose string vibrates slowly and gives a low note. Remember: loudness is about the size of the vibration, and pitch is about the speed of the vibration. These are two separate properties, and a sound can be loud and low, quiet and high, or any other combination.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Some flying insects, like mosquitoes, make a high buzzing sound purely because their wings beat hundreds of times every second. The faster the wingbeat, the higher the buzz you hear near your ear at night. This is also why protecting yourself from mosquitoes with a net matters: the buzz is harmless, but the bite can carry malaria.

concepts.title: How a Sound Wave Travels
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to a deeper question. When the muadhin calls the adhan at the mosque, how does that sound reach your house far away? The vibration happens at the mosque, but you hear it in your home. Something must carry the sound across the distance. That something is a sound wave.

Here is how it works, step by step. When an object vibrates, it moves forwards and pushes the air particles in front of it. Those particles get squeezed together for a moment. Then the object moves back, and the particles spread out again. But here is the clever part: the squeezed particles bump into the particles next to them and pass the push along. Those particles bump the next ones, and so on, and so on, like a message passed from hand to hand down a long line of people. In this way the vibration travels outward through the air as a sound wave, even though each particle only moves a tiny bit backwards and forwards and then stays roughly where it was.

This is a very important idea, so let us be clear about it. The particles themselves do not travel all the way from the mosque to your house. The air does not fly across the town. Instead, each particle nudges the next one, and it is the vibration, the energy, that travels. Think of a long line of children standing shoulder to shoulder. If the first child gently sways and bumps the next, the bump can pass all the way down the line, but no single child leaves their place. That is exactly how a sound wave moves through the air.

Sound travels quickly, but not instantly. In air, sound travels at about 343 metres every second. That is fast, but light is far faster. This is why, during a thunderstorm over the coast near Berbera or Mombasa, you see the flash of lightning first and hear the thunder a few seconds later, even though they happen at the same moment. The light reaches you almost instantly, but the sound takes time to travel to your ears.

Sound Needs a Medium — Solids, Liquids and Gases

Because a sound wave works by making particles vibrate, sound can only travel through a substance that has particles. The substance that a sound wave travels through is called the medium. Solids, liquids and gases can all be a medium for sound, because all of them are made of particles.

You can prove sound travels through a solid with a simple test. Tap gently on one end of a wooden table or bench and ask a friend to listen normally, then ask them to press their ear flat against the table and listen to the same tap again. The tap sounds clearer and stronger through the solid wood, because the particles in a solid are packed tightly together and pass the vibration along very efficiently. Sound also travels well through liquids. This is how whales and dolphins in the Indian Ocean communicate over long distances, singing to one another through the water. And of course sound travels through the gas we call air, which is how you hear almost everything in daily life.

Now for one of the most surprising facts in all of science. A vacuum is a space with no particles at all. Outer space is very close to a perfect vacuum. Because there are no particles in a vacuum, there is nothing to vibrate, and so a sound wave cannot form or travel. This means space is completely silent.

Think about what that means. If two astronauts on the Moon stood right next to each other and one hammered on a rock, the other would not hear a single sound through the space around them, because the Moon has almost no air. This is why astronauts talk to each other using radios, which send the message as radio waves that can cross a vacuum, not as sound. In science-fiction films you often see huge explosions in space with a loud 'BOOM'. Now you know the truth: a real explosion in space would make no sound at all, because there is no medium to carry the wave. The film-makers add the sound only because it is dramatic.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Scientists think that if space were full of air, the Sun would fill the whole sky with a constant deep humming sound, so loud it would never stop. Because space is a vacuum, we live under a silent Sun, and the only sound near you at midday is the world of the Earth around you.

concepts.title: Echoes: Sound That Bounces Back
concepts.explanation:
One special property of all waves is that they can be reflected, which means they bounce off a surface, just as a football bounces back off a wall. Because sound is a wave, sound can be reflected too. A reflected sound wave has a special name: an echo.

Sound reflects best from large, smooth, hard, flat surfaces such as a concrete wall, a cliff face, tiles or glass. If you stand in a big empty room with bare walls and clap your hands once, the sound seems to last longer and then fade, because the clap keeps bouncing between the walls. If you shout across a rocky valley in the volcanic highlands, your voice can travel to a far cliff, reflect, and come back to you a moment later, and you hear your own words returning. That returning sound is the echo.

Echoes can be very useful. Bats hunting insects at dusk send out sounds and listen for the echo bouncing off an insect; from the time the echo takes to return, the bat works out exactly where its food is. Fishing boats and ships use the same idea, called sonar or echo-sounding: they send a sound down into the water and time how long the echo takes to bounce back from the seabed, which tells them how deep the water is or whether there is a school of fish below. Doctors use echoes of very high sounds to make pictures of an unborn baby inside the mother, which is called an ultrasound scan. In each case, the sound must travel to the object and then back again, so the sound travels double the distance to the object.

But echoes are not always wanted. When musicians record a song, strong echoes make the sound messy and unclear. In a theatre or a large hall, echoes can make a speaker's voice hard to understand. To stop unwanted echoes, people cover the walls with soft, uneven materials such as thick curtains, foam or carpet. Soft materials absorb the sound instead of reflecting it, so the echo dies away. This is why a room full of soft cushions and hanging cloth sounds quiet and 'dead', while an empty tiled bathroom makes your voice ring.
concepts.example: Sound is energy, and very loud sounds carry a lot of energy. The strong vibrations of a very loud sound can actually damage the delicate parts inside your ears, sometimes permanently. This is why people who work near very loud machines, like aeroplane engines or heavy generators, wear ear protection. You should protect your own ears too: do not stand right next to very loud loudspeakers for a long time, and never play music at full volume through earphones. Your hearing is a precious gift, and once it is damaged it usually cannot be repaired. Looking after your body is part of being a responsible steward of what you have been given.

concepts.title: Inside the Earth
concepts.explanation:
We now leave sound behind and travel downwards, deep into the ground beneath your feet. Have you ever wondered what is inside the Earth? You cannot dig down to find out, because the centre of the Earth is far too deep and far too hot. Yet scientists have worked out what the inside of the Earth is like, and they have also worked out that the Earth is about 4500 million years old, which is an almost unimaginable length of time.

If you could slice the Earth in half like a giant fruit, you would see that it is made of layers, one inside the other. Let us travel from the outside in.

The crust is the thin outer layer of solid rock. This is the ground you walk on, farm, and build your home upon, whether in Garissa, Dar es Salaam or Lamu. Compared with the whole Earth, the crust is very thin, like the skin on a fruit.

The mantle lies just below the crust. It is a very thick layer of extremely hot rock. Most of the mantle is solid, but it is so hot that it can slowly flow, a little like very thick honey moving over a long time. Hot molten rock in and below the crust is called magma.

The outer core is deeper still. It is made of the metals iron and nickel, and it is so hot that these metals are molten (melted into a liquid).

The inner core is right at the centre. It is also made of iron and nickel, but even though it is the hottest part of all, the enormous pressure squeezing it keeps it solid.

So from the surface to the centre the order is: crust, mantle, outer core, inner core. A good way to remember the two cores is that the outer core is liquid metal and the inner core is solid metal, kept solid by the crushing pressure at the very heart of the planet.

The rocks of the crust are made of many chemical elements. The most common element in the crust is the non-metal oxygen, locked inside the rocks, and the most common metal is aluminium. Other common elements include silicon, iron and calcium. So the ground is not just 'dirt', it is a rich mixture of elements, some of which we dig up and use to build and to make tools.

Did You Know? The temperature at the centre of the Earth is thought to be about 5000 to 6000 degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun. Even so, the inner core stays solid because it is squeezed by the unimaginable weight of everything above it.

Here is a strange and wonderful idea: the continents are slowly moving. Long ago, people believed the Earth had always looked exactly as it does now. But in 1912 a German scientist named Alfred Wegener suggested that, millions of years ago, all the land on Earth was joined together in one giant continent. Over a very long time this super-continent broke apart and the pieces slowly drifted away from one another to where they are today. This idea is called continental drift.

What made Wegener think of such a bold idea? He noticed evidence:

The shapes of the continents seem to fit together like pieces of a jigsaw. Look at a map: the bulge of West Africa fits neatly into the curve of South America.

The types of rock on the edges of continents that would once have been joined match each other closely.

The fossils of the same ancient plants and animals are found on continents that are now separated by wide oceans, as if they had once lived on the same land.

At first many people did not believe Wegener, because he could not explain how the continents moved. Today we understand the answer. The Earth's crust is not one solid shell; it is cracked into enormous pieces called tectonic plates. These plates float on the hot, slowly flowing rock of the mantle beneath them, and they move, carrying the continents and oceans on their backs. Some plates sit under the oceans (oceanic plates) and some carry the continents (continental plates). Most of East Africa, including Somalia, Kenya and Tanzania, sits on the great African plate.

The plates move incredibly slowly, only about 4 centimetres each year, which is about the same speed as your fingernails grow. You will never feel this movement, but over millions of years it is enough to tear continents apart and build mountains.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Right here in East Africa, the African plate is very slowly splitting into two along the Great Rift Valley. Scientists say that in millions of years, a new ocean could open where the Rift Valley is today, dividing the land we know.

concepts.title: When the Earth Changes: Mountains, Volcanoes and Earthquakes
concepts.explanation:
The places where two tectonic plates meet are called plate boundaries, and these are the most exciting and sometimes the most dangerous places on Earth. Because the plates are always moving, most big geological changes happen at plate boundaries. Some changes are very slow, taking millions of years, while others are sudden and violent. There are three main things plates can do when they meet.

When two plates push together, one plate can be forced down underneath the other. This is called subduction. The rock that is pushed down into the hot mantle melts and becomes part of the mantle. Sometimes, instead of one sliding under, the plates crumple against each other and the rock layers are squeezed and folded upwards into fold mountains. The mighty Himalayas and the Rocky Mountains were built this way, folded up like a rug pushed against a wall.

When two plates pull apart, the crust cracks and stretches until it becomes too thin. Hot molten rock from the mantle rises up through the cracks and erupts at the surface as lava, which cools and hardens into new rock. This builds volcanoes and makes brand-new crust. This is exactly what is happening along the Great Rift Valley, where the plate is stretching and volcanoes have grown.

When two plates slide past each other, they do not move smoothly. The plates are huge and heavy, and there is a great deal of friction between them, so they stick together. But the forces keep pushing, and pressure builds up and up, just like bending a stick further and further. Eventually the pressure is too great and the plates suddenly jerk free, releasing all that stored energy at once. This sudden violent movement of the crust is an earthquake.

A volcano forms where magma (molten rock underground) rises up through cracks in the crust and reaches the surface. Remember the important pair of words: molten rock is called magma while it is underground, and lava once it comes out onto the surface. When a volcano erupts, lava and ash pour or shoot out, then cool and harden into new rock. Because each eruption adds another layer, the volcano grows a little bigger every time it erupts.

Some eruptions are gentle, but if the magma is thick and full of dissolved gas, the pressure can build until the eruption is enormously violent, blasting rock, ash and gas high into the sky. A violent eruption near the sea can even trigger a tsunami, a giant wave. Scientists describe volcanoes with three useful words: an active volcano may erupt at any time; a dormant (or inactive) volcano has not erupted for a very long time but still could; and an extinct volcano will never erupt again because its supply of magma is finished. The main parts of a volcano include the magma chamber below, the main vent through which magma rises, the crater at the top, and the lava flow and ash cloud that escape during an eruption.
concepts.example: Some earthquakes are so gentle that only sensitive instruments can detect them, while others are violent enough to crack roads and knock down buildings. The strength of an earthquake is called its magnitude, which is a number that lets scientists compare one earthquake with another. The magnitude depends on how big the stuck section of the plates is, and on how far the rocks jump when they finally break free. In the very largest earthquakes, the rocks can move tens of metres in just a few seconds.

concepts.title: The Sun, the Moon and Eclipses
concepts.explanation:
Now we look up. The Sun is a star that gives out its own light. The Moon does not give out any light of its own; we only see the Moon because sunlight bounces off it. Both the Earth and the Moon are opaque, which means light cannot pass through them. Whenever an opaque object blocks light, it casts a shadow, an area where the light has been blocked.

Light is important to understand here, so remember one rule: light travels in straight lines, which we call rays. Because light travels in straight lines and cannot bend around an object, an opaque object always leaves a dark shadow behind it on the side away from the light. An aeroplane flying over the savanna casts a moving shadow on the ground below, because its metal body blocks the Sun's rays. An eclipse is really just a very large and dramatic shadow made in space by the Sun, Moon and Earth.
concepts.example: Light is important to understand here, so remember one rule: light travels in straight lines, which we call rays. An eclipse is really just a very large and dramatic shadow made in space by the Sun, Moon and Earth.

methods.title: The Ruler and the Rubber Band: Making Sound
methods.example: To show that sound is made by vibrations, and to explore what changes the loudness and the pitch of a sound.
steps: Hold the ruler firmly on the table so that most of it sticks out over the edge.
Twang the free end so it vibrates. Watch it move and listen to the sound.
Now slide the ruler so that only a short part sticks out. Twang it again.
Repeat with a long part sticking out. Listen carefully to how the pitch changes.
Next, stretch the rubber band between your fingers, or over an empty tin, and pluck it gently, then pluck it harder. Listen to the loudness.

methods.title: The String Telephone: Sound Through a Solid
methods.example: To show that sound needs vibrations and a medium to travel, and that sound can travel well through a solid string.
steps: Carefully make a small hole in the bottom of each cup with the sharp point. Push away from your hand and ask an adult to help.
Thread the string through both holes so the open ends of the cups face away from each other.
Tie a knot inside each cup so the string cannot slip out.
Give one cup to your partner and walk apart until the string is pulled tight.
One person speaks quietly into their cup while the other holds their cup over their ear and listens.

methods.title: Hunting for Echoes
methods.example: To find out which places and surfaces produce the clearest echoes, and to understand reflection of sound.
steps: Stand in an empty room with hard, bare walls. Clap once, sharply. Listen for the sound lasting or bouncing.
Move to a room with soft furniture, curtains or cushions. Clap the same way and listen.
Go outside into an open space with no walls nearby. Clap and listen.
If it is safe, stand a good distance from a large flat wall and clap or shout, listening for the echo returning.
Record how strong the echo was in each place.

methods.title: The Ball-and-Torch Eclipse Model
methods.example: To model how solar and lunar eclipses happen using a torch and two balls of different sizes.
steps: Darken the room. Place the large ball (Earth) on a cup or bowl so it does not roll.
Shine the torch (Sun) at the Earth from about half a metre away. Notice one side is lit (day) and one side is dark (night).
Solar eclipse: hold the small ball (Moon) between the torch and the Earth. Look for the small shadow of the Moon falling on the Earth.
Move the Moon slightly and watch the shadow move across the surface of the Earth.
Lunar eclipse: now move the Moon to the far side of the Earth, into the Earth's shadow. Watch the Earth's shadow fall on the Moon.

workedExamples.title: Timing an Echo
workedExamples.prompt: Some questions about sound involve a calculation. Let us work through one carefully, showing every step, so you can follow the method.
workedExamples.solution:
Problem: Halima stands in a valley and shouts towards a tall cliff. She hears the echo return exactly 2 seconds later. Sound travels at about 343 metres per second in air. How far away is the cliff?

Step 1 — Find the total distance the sound travelled. We use the rule distance = speed x time. The sound travelled for 2 seconds at 343 metres per second, so distance = 343 x 2 = 686 metres.

Step 2 — Remember the sound made a round trip. The 686 metres is the distance to the cliff and back again. To find the distance to the cliff alone, we must halve it: 686 / 2 = 343 metres.

Answer: The cliff is about 343 metres away. The key idea to remember is that an echo always travels double the distance to the surface, so you divide the total by two to find the one-way distance.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: What is needed for a sound to be made? A) heat B) light C) a vibration D) a magnet
workedExamples.solution: 1 C A vibration is always needed to make a sound; heat, light and magnets do not make sound by themselves.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: A guitar makes a sound mainly because: A) it is made of wood B) its strings vibrate C) there is air inside D) it has metal parts
workedExamples.solution: 2 B It is the vibrating strings that make the note, not the wood or the metal parts.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Sound travels through air as a: A) current B) stream C) wind D) wave
workedExamples.solution: 3 D Sound travels through air as a sound wave, passed particle to particle.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Which of these can sound NOT travel through? A) solid B) liquid C) gas D) vacuum
workedExamples.solution: 4 D A vacuum has no particles, so there is nothing to vibrate and carry the sound.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: The pitch of a sound depends on: A) how big the vibration is B) how fast the object vibrates C) the colour of the object D) the temperature
workedExamples.solution: 5 B Pitch depends on how fast the object vibrates; faster vibration gives a higher pitch.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: A reflected sound wave is called: A) an echo B) a shadow C) a medium D) a ray
workedExamples.solution: 6 A A reflected sound wave is called an echo.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: Which surface gives the BEST echo? A) thick carpet B) soft curtain C) glass window D) wool blanket
workedExamples.solution: 7 C Hard, smooth, flat surfaces like glass reflect sound best; soft materials absorb it.

activities.title: The Ruler and the Rubber Band: Making Sound
activities.materials: A plastic or wooden ruler (or a flat stick).; A sturdy table or desk edge.; A rubber band (an elastic band).; An empty tin, cup or small box to stretch the band over (optional).
steps: Hold the ruler firmly on the table so that most of it sticks out over the edge.
Twang the free end so it vibrates. Watch it move and listen to the sound.
Now slide the ruler so that only a short part sticks out. Twang it again.
Repeat with a long part sticking out. Listen carefully to how the pitch changes.
Next, stretch the rubber band between your fingers, or over an empty tin, and pluck it gently, then pluck it harder. Listen to the loudness.

activities.title: The String Telephone: Sound Through a Solid
activities.materials: Two empty tins, paper cups or plastic cups.; A long piece of string (as long as a room if possible).; A sharp point (a nail or pencil tip) to make a small hole — ask an adult.; A partner to talk to.
steps: Carefully make a small hole in the bottom of each cup with the sharp point. Push away from your hand and ask an adult to help.
Thread the string through both holes so the open ends of the cups face away from each other.
Tie a knot inside each cup so the string cannot slip out.
Give one cup to your partner and walk apart until the string is pulled tight.
One person speaks quietly into their cup while the other holds their cup over their ear and listens.

activities.title: Hunting for Echoes
activities.materials: Your own hands (for clapping) or your voice.; Access to different spaces: an empty room with bare walls, a room with curtains and cushions, an open outdoor space, and if possible a spot near a large wall or cliff.; A notebook to record what you hear.
steps: Stand in an empty room with hard, bare walls. Clap once, sharply. Listen for the sound lasting or bouncing.
Move to a room with soft furniture, curtains or cushions. Clap the same way and listen.
Go outside into an open space with no walls nearby. Clap and listen.
If it is safe, stand a good distance from a large flat wall and clap or shout, listening for the echo returning.
Record how strong the echo was in each place.

activities.title: The Ball-and-Torch Eclipse Model
activities.materials: A torch or a phone light (this is the Sun).; A large ball, such as a football or a large orange (this is the Earth).; A small ball, such as a tennis ball, a lime or a small stone (this is the Moon).; A dark room. Close the curtains or work at night.
steps: Darken the room. Place the large ball (Earth) on a cup or bowl so it does not roll.
Shine the torch (Sun) at the Earth from about half a metre away. Notice one side is lit (day) and one side is dark (night).
Solar eclipse: hold the small ball (Moon) between the torch and the Earth. Look for the small shadow of the Moon falling on the Earth.
Move the Moon slightly and watch the shadow move across the surface of the Earth.
Lunar eclipse: now move the Moon to the far side of the Earth, into the Earth's shadow. Watch the Earth's shadow fall on the Moon.

activities.title: Observe: When the Earth Changes: Mountains, Volcanoes and Earthquakes
activities.materials: A plastic or wooden ruler (or a flat stick).; A sturdy table or desk edge.; A rubber band (an elastic band).; An empty tin, cup or small box to stretch the band over (optional).
steps: Look for an example of when the earth changes: mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Vibrate and Sound wave.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

activities.title: Sort: The Sun, the Moon and Eclipses
activities.materials: Two empty tins, paper cups or plastic cups.; A long piece of string (as long as a room if possible).; A sharp point (a nail or pencil tip) to make a small hole — ask an adult.; A partner to talk to.
steps: Look for an example of the sun, the moon and eclipses around your home or outside.
Find examples at home and sort them into groups, then explain your rule.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Vibrate and Sound wave.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Sound Needs Vibration and a Medium
rules.text: To hear a sound you need TWO things: 1. Something vibrating to make the sound. 2. A medium of particles (solid, liquid or gas) for the wave to travel through. No vibration, or no medium, means no sound.

rules.title: Three Plate Movements, Three Results
rules.text: Three plate movements, three results: Plates pushing together -> fold mountains (and subduction). Plates pulling apart -> volcanoes and new crust. Plates sliding past -> earthquakes. Magma is underground; lava is on the surface.

terms: Vibrate
To move backwards and forwards very quickly.
Sound wave
Vibrations of particles that carry sound energy from a source to your ear.
Medium
The substance (solid, liquid or gas) a wave travels through.
Particles
The tiny pieces that all substances are made from.
Vacuum
A space with no particles at all; sound cannot travel through it.
Pitch
How high or low a sound is; depends on how FAST something vibrates.
Loudness (volume)
How loud or quiet a sound is; depends on how BIG the vibration is.
Echo
A sound wave reflected back from a surface.
Reflected
Bounced back after meeting a surface.
Crust
The thin, solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth.
Mantle
The thick, mostly solid layer below the crust that can flow slowly.
Magma
Molten rock while it is underground.

connections.text: the particle model explains both how sound travels and why the Earth has solid and liquid layers.
sound is one way energy is transferred; volcanoes and earthquakes release stored energy from inside the Earth.
eclipses depend on light travelling in straight lines and being blocked by opaque objects, which links to the study of light and shadows.
the movement of the Sun, Earth and Moon connects to day and night, the seasons, gravity and tides.
plate boundaries, the Great Rift Valley, mountains and volcanoes link science to the land of East Africa.
the lunar (Hijri) calendar, moon sighting for Ramadan and Eid, and the eclipse prayer (salat al-kusuf) connect the sky to daily worship.

realProblems.prompt: The adhan is called from a tall minaret in Hargeisa and is heard across the town. Explain how the sound reaches homes far away, using the idea of a sound wave and a medium.
realProblems.answer: 1 The vibrating voice/loudspeaker makes the air particles vibrate. The vibration passes from particle to particle as a sound wave through the air (the medium), spreading outward in all directions until it reaches the ears of people far away.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Vibrate, Sound wave, Medium — then explain your reasoning step by step.

The vibration passes from particle to particle as a sound wave through the air (the medium), spreading outward in all directions until it reaches the ears of people far away.

realProblems.prompt: Amina presses her ear to a wooden bench and hears a tap much more clearly than through the air. Explain why.
realProblems.answer: 2 Wood is a solid, and its particles are packed tightly together, so they pass the vibration along more efficiently than the loosely spaced particles in air. The sound is therefore clearer through the bench.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Vibrate, Sound wave, Medium — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: 2 Wood is a solid, and its particles are packed tightly together, so they pass the vibration along more efficiently than the loosely spaced particles in air. The sound is therefore clearer through the bench.

realProblems.prompt: A fisherman on the Indian Ocean coast uses an echo-sounder to find the depth of water. If the sound takes time to go down and come back, explain why he must remember the sound travels the distance twice.
realProblems.answer: 3 The sound must travel down to the seabed and then reflect back up to the boat, so it covers the distance twice. To find the true depth, the total distance must be halved.
realProblems.hint: Decide which idea the situation is about — Vibrate, Sound wave, Medium — then explain your reasoning step by step.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Check your reasoning against this: 3 The sound must travel down to the seabed and then reflect back up to the boat, so it covers the distance twice. To find the true depth, the total distance must be halved.

realProblems.prompt: People living near the Great Rift Valley sometimes feel tremors and see volcanoes. Explain what is happening to the tectonic plates in that region.
realProblems.answer: 4 The African plate is slowly splitting along the Rift Valley. As the plates pull apart, magma rises to form volcanoes, and the shifting and sticking of the plates releases pressure as earthquakes/tremors.

realProblems.answer: 5 A lunar eclipse only involves the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon, so looking at the dim Moon is safe. A solar eclipse involves looking towards the Sun, whose light can permanently damage or blind the eyes, so it must never be viewed directly.

rounds.explanation: The inner core is solid metal (iron and nickel), kept solid by huge pressure.

rounds.prompt: Molten rock on the surface of the Earth is called:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Molten rock is called lava on the surface and magma underground.

rounds.prompt: Sound travels through air as a:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Sound travels through air as a sound wave, passed particle to particle.

games.title: Think Fast: Loudness (volume)
games.description: Practise loudness (volume) through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which surface gives the BEST echo?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Hard, smooth, flat surfaces like glass reflect sound best; soft materials absorb it.

rounds.prompt: Tectonic plates move at about the speed that:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Plates move only about 4 cm a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.

rounds.prompt: What is needed for a sound to be made?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A vibration is always needed to make a sound; heat, light and magnets do not make sound by themselves.

rounds.prompt: Which of these can sound NOT travel through?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: A vacuum has no particles, so there is nothing to vibrate and carry the sound.

games.title: Explain It: Echo
games.description: Practise echo through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: The layers of the Earth from the outside inwards are:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: The correct order from outside to centre is crust, mantle, core.

rounds.prompt: An earthquake is caused when plates:
choices: stick, build up pressure, then suddenly slip
rounds.answer: stick, build up pressure, then suddenly slip
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Plates stick due to friction, pressure builds, then they suddenly slip: an earthquake.

rounds.prompt: A guitar makes a sound mainly because:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: It is the vibrating strings that make the note, not the wood or the metal parts.

rounds.prompt: The pitch of a sound depends on:
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 6 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: Pitch depends on how fast the object vibrates; faster vibration gives a higher pitch.

selfAssessment: I can explain that sound is made by vibrations and describe how those vibrations start.
I can describe how a sound wave travels by making particles vibrate backwards and forwards.
I can state that sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases, but not through a vacuum, and explain why.
I can describe how sound waves are reflected to make echoes, and give useful and unwanted examples.
I can distinguish between loudness (volume) and pitch, and connect each to the vibration.
I can describe the structure of the Earth: crust, mantle, outer core and inner core.
I can explain the evidence for continental drift and describe tectonic plates.
I can explain how fold mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes form at plate boundaries.
